news.title: South Korea and US vow close cooperation on North Korea
news.text:
WASHINGTON: South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke on Monday (Aug 24), and Seoul said they agreed to maintain close communication and cooperation on resolving the North Korean nuclear issue, South Korea's Yonhap news agency reported.

The US State Department issued only a brief statement on the phone call, which comes at a period of tension between the allies. President Donald Trump recently announced a scaling back of joint military exercises and praised nuclear-armed North Korea, while saying that Seoul had not helped his efforts to try to denuclearise Iran.

The State Department said Rubio and Cho discussed "a range of issues in the US-ROK Alliance", referring to South Korea by the initials of its official name, the Republic of Korea.

"The Secretary noted the need for the two countries to remain in close coordination on matters that are integral to the Alliance," it added.

Yonhap said that in a statement on their talks, South Korea's Foreign Ministry did not mention whether the diplomats reaffirmed their usual commitment to North Korea's denuclearisation, despite their emphasis on the importance of cooperation on the North Korean nuclear issue.

"The minister and secretary agreed to continue close communication and cooperation between South Korea and the US for peace on the Korean Peninsula and the resolution of North Korea's nuclear issue while maintaining a solid combined defence posture," Yonhap quoted the ministry release as saying.

It cited Cho as saying that Seoul would do its best to help ensure Trump's recent message for North Korea would lead to the resumption of dialogue between Washington and Pyongyang, and peace on the peninsula.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump's olive branch to North Korea's Kim Jong Un last week, coupled with his criticism of Seoul, has raised concern among analysts that Trump's unpredictability could strain alliances that have long maintained peace in Asia.

news.title: US-Canada trade war escalates as Trump announces 50% tariffs on vehicles
news.text:
US-Canada trade war has escalated sharply, with US President Donald Trump on Monday announcing that tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel imports will be raised to 50 per cent from January 2027, following the collapse of trade negotiations between Washington and Ottawa last week, reported ANI.

Trump announced in a post on Truth Social, accusing Canada of imposing high tariffs on American farmers and agricultural products and warning that companies manufacturing in the United States would face zero tariffs.

"Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years. Their ridiculously high tariffs on our Farmers and farm products has made life impossible for these great American Patriots, and has long created a 60 Billion Dollar Deficit between our two Countries. Not sustainable, and NOT ANYMORE! On January First, 2027, Tariffs on all Cars, Trucks, both large and small, Automotive Parts, and Steel, will be increased to 50%. Build in the U.S. and there are ZERO TARIFFS. Canada will be treated like a State no longer!" Trump said in his post.

The US President further accused Canada of being among the most difficult countries to deal with in trade, arguing that Ottawa depends heavily on the American market while claiming the US does not similarly rely on Canada.

"On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON'T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite! Thank you for your attention to this matter!" he added.

The announcement came after trade negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney describing the US' last-minute proposed terms as "unfair" and "uneconomic". Canada has said it will respond with retaliatory tariffs on US goods.

Carney said he had instructed Canadian negotiators to return to Ottawa after more than a year of discussions with Washington, arguing that Canada could not accept the US offer.

"Late last evening I instructed our negotiators to return to Ottawa. We cannot accept what the U.S. has offered, and we will not give what they have asked," Carney said on Saturday.

He added that Canada would match the new US tariffs dollar-for-dollar to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.

"Canada will match the U.S.' new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses. We take this step confident that it is in the best interests of Canada," Carney added.

Canada's retaliatory measures are expected to take effect on September 8, with Ottawa targeting a range of US products, including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.

The latest escalation follows the United States imposing 50 per cent tariffs on roughly USD 20 billion worth of Canadian imports after the trade talks failed.

The measures affect five per cent of Canada's exports to the United States.

Carney said Canada's negotiators had made progress during the discussions but that Washington's final changes undermined the possibility of reaching an agreement.

"Last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," he said.

The Canadian Prime Minister said Ottawa would also introduce additional measures to support workers and businesses.

"We have recognised from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship," Carney said.

Carney also said Canada was working to strengthen its domestic economy and diversify its export markets. He said the country was advancing nearly USD 500 billion in major infrastructure projects and seeking new export markets for Canadian businesses.

"Our existing free trade deals already provide Canada with preferential access to 1.5 billion consumers, and we are on track to double that market access by the end of this year," he said.

The United States Trade Representative, meanwhile, criticised Canada's decision to suspend negotiations, calling it a missed opportunity and accusing Ottawa of withdrawing commitments and introducing new demands during the talks.

The US said it had offered Canada sector-specific relief involving steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber, along with cooperation on export controls, digital trade, critical minerals and supply chain coordination.

"Despite the US offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walkbacks of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," the US Trade Representative said.

Trump has earlier slammed Ottawa, referring to Canada as an American state, following the suspension of trade talks and Carney calling the US terms "uneconomic, unfair, and undermining the net benefits" for the country.

In a separate post on Truth Social, making them his first remarks since Carney announced that Ottawa will match the new US tariffs "dollar-for-dollar", Trump argued that Canada has charged massive tariffs on American farmers.

"Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!! They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!! President DJT," the post read.

The latest dispute adds to already strained relations between Washington and Ottawa, with Trump repeatedly criticising Canada's trade policies and reviving his description of Canada as a potential US state.

The new tariff announcement further raises uncertainty for industries deeply integrated across the US-Canada border.

news.title: US proposes H-1B visa fee exceeding $100,000 on new grounds
news.text:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Monday proposed a 103,265-U.S.-dollar fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions, marking the agency's newest move to restrict the visa program on new grounds, reported Xinhua.

 The move came after previous efforts to charge 100,000 dollars for the visa were struck down by the courts.

 "The proposed fee would generate revenue to recover a portion of the federal government's costs for administering the lawful immigration system," the DHS said in a news release.

 The new fee is designed to recover a portion of the full costs of providing immigration adjudication and naturalization services incurred by multiple federal agencies in processing, adjudicating and supporting the lawful immigration system, according to a document scheduled to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday.

 The DHS estimates the proposed fee would generate approximately 8.8 billion dollars annually, based on a projected annual volume of 85,000 H-1B cap-subject petitions, according to the release.

 Under the proposed rule, the additional fee would not apply to H-1B petitions that are not subject to the cap, such as petitions filed by certain nonprofit research organizations, governmental research organizations, and institutions of higher education, the release added.

 The public will be given a 30-day period to submit comments on the proposed rule before it can take effect.

 "If finalized, the new proposal would place a significant new burden on the technology and finance sectors, which rely on the H-1B visa to hire top international graduates from U.S. universities," The Wall Street Journal reported.

 The latest proposal came two months after the Trump administration's 100,000-dollar fee on new H-1B visas was struck down by a federal judge in Boston, Massachusetts. The judge ruled that the executive branch exceeded its authority and violated the Administrative Procedure Act.

 In September 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation raising the fee that companies pay to sponsor H-1B applicants to 100,000 dollars, saying the move was intended to ensure that the United States brings in highly skilled talent whom American workers cannot replace.

 Earlier reports from U.S. media noted that the hefty fee would affect tech giants such as Amazon, Microsoft and Google, which have long relied on the H-1B visa program to hire foreign employees, including software developers.

 CBS reported that the plan could backfire by encouraging U.S. companies to shift jobs overseas, especially in specialized fields such as research and development. It could also further deter international students from studying in the United States.

 Since Trump returned to the White House, his administration has tightened immigration policies, cracking down on undocumented immigrants and increasing scrutiny of U.S. visa holders.

 On Aug. 10, the U.S. State Department announced that it had revoked more than 175,000 visas since January 2025, when Trump began his second term.

 The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States, according to a report by The Associated Press.

 "If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in U.S. history and would likely face legal challenges," the report said.

news.text:
The US Supreme Court has cleared the way for Donald Trump to restrict mail-in voting.

The ruling on Monday marks a temporary victory for the US president, but it is unclear how much his administration will be able to change before the fast-approaching midterm elections.

Mr Trump has long claimed that mail-in ballots are vulnerable to fraud, despite strong evidence suggesting the opposite and his own use of the voting method.

Democrats have accused the president of laying the groundwork to discredit the results of the November elections, in which Republicans are widely expected to lose control of Congress.

The restrictions are part of his aggressive push to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, which would also require proof of citizenship to vote, despite non-citizen voting being considered rare.

His executive order, signed in March, calls on his administration to create lists of eligible voters and orders the US Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to people on those lists.

It was met with swift legal challenges. Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia sued to block the order.

They argued that the US Constitution gives states the power to run elections – not the federal government – and that Mr Trump's changes could lead to chaos and partisan abuse.

The Supreme Court's conservative majority ruled that the states did not have the legal right to challenge it, allowing parts to go ahead, for now.

Letitia James, the New York attorney general, foreshadowed more legal wrangling, calling the decision a "painful setback" but vowing it would "not be the final word".

"The District Court lacked jurisdiction to bar the Government from trying to implement" the executive order, the Supreme Court majority said.

It did not rule on the legality of the order, adding that a final judgment has not been made.

The three liberal justices on the nine-member Supreme Court dissented.

Mr Trump – who voted by mail in Florida's Republican primary this month – has repeatedly blamed mail voting, without credible evidence, for his loss to Joe Biden in 2020.

"Mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt," he said during a July speech on election security.

Mail-in ballots are popular with voters of both parties, with roughly 30 per cent of votes cast that way in the 2024 presidential election.
news.author: Iona Cleave

news.title: US Proposes Raising H-1B Visa Fee to Over US$103,000
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - The US Department of Homeland Security has proposed raising the filing fee for H-1B work visas to over US$103,000 (Rp1.82 billion)."The Department of Homeland Security proposes setting a fee of US$103,265, payable at the time of registration, for all H-1B visa filings," according to a document obtained by RIA Novosti, as cited by Antara.The unreleased document also notes that this fee—amounting to hundreds of thousands of dollars—"would be charged in addition to all other applicable fees or payments."The document states that the fee is intended to cover a portion of the costs associated with visa processing.The H-1B is a visa category that allows US employers to hire foreign nationals for specialized professions requiring "extraordinary aptitude and ability," as determined by US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).Meanwhile, last June, a US federal judge ruled that President Donald Trump's decision to set a US$100,000 fee constituted an unlawful tax levy.Subsequently, in July, Vice President JD Vance stated that the US Department of Labor was investigating dozens of alleged fraud cases involving the H-1B work visa program and had issued a number of subpoenas.Vance argued that the misuse of H-1B visas suppresses wages for US workers. news.title: UK’s Burnham plans US trip in September to lobby Trump on Ukraine needs
news.text:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he and other European leaders plan to travel to the US next month to lobby President Donald Trump to let Ukraine access some of its Patriot air defence missile stocks ahead of the winter.
“I’m looking forward to going to New York in September,” Burnham said in an interview with Bloomberg in Kyiv on Monday evening, referring to the coming UN General Assembly meeting in New York. It would be his first trip to the US since becoming prime minister.
“I’ve not fully confirmed the details yet but it’s likely I will go, particularly after today’s discussion,” he said. “Leaving today, I’m quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks.”
Burnham’s comments came on his first international visit since becoming premier, after chairing a meeting of Ukraine’s allies for the first time and holding a bilateral meeting with Ukraine’s President, Volodymyr Zelensky.
Zelensky has made repeated pleas to European nations and the US to help Ukraine obtain Patriot missile interceptors and to replenish its stocks in time for winter, when Russia is expected to ramp up attacks on energy infrastructure again. The interceptors are the most potent weapons to shoot down Russian cruise and ballistic missiles.
Burnham said he left feeling “really optimistic” that Ukraine’s current struggles defending against Russian ballistic missile strikes due to its low stockpile of interceptors are “fixable”.
He said European leaders were considering holding another Coalition of the Willing meeting around the UN General Assembly meeting with a view towards securing American interceptors and stocks from other countries.
“That would seem to be the most likely pace of direction,” Burnham said. “Not confirmed yet but that seemed like where most people’s minds were going.”
He stressed that while the UK did not use the Patriot missiles required by Ukraine, other European nations needed to step up.

“There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with,” Burnham said. “It’s probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation.”
Trump has backtracked on an earlier promise to provide or let Kyiv build interceptors for US-made Patriot missile defence systems. The war in Iran has also seriously depleted global stocks of Patriot missiles, leading to delays in supplies and making allies reluctant to provide them to Kyiv.
Trump in July told reporters he had not yet agreed to Ukraine’s request to build Patriot missiles. “We’re talking about it but it’s a hard thing to give away that kind of technology,” he said at the time.
Burnham, in contrast, has moved aggressively to allow Ukraine access to closely guarded British defence technology.
The UK prime minister will allow Ukraine access to classified information on British components for the long-range missile, called SCALP, allowing Kyiv to assemble the cruise missile in Ukraine.
“We value the fact that the UK’s course remains unchanged – full support for Ukraine and our defence,” Zelensky said in a post on social media late on Monday outlining his discussions with Burnham.
Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that he is seeking 300 Patriot missiles for the winter. He has said previously that if Kyiv could buy 5 per cent of the United States’ Patriot missile stockpile it would survive the winter, and if it could purchase 10 per cent it could destroy all of Russia’s ballistic missiles.
Ukraine has already been struggling with an onslaught of Russian ballistic attacks that have led to a rising death toll among its population.
At least 437 Ukrainian civilians were killed in July 2026, a 30 per cent increase on a year earlier, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine. August has seen several Russian attacks with high civilian death tolls, with 15 killed in ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv on Thursday and 16 killed in a drone attack on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih on Friday.

news.title: Canada to hit U.S. with retaliatory tariffs as trade war escalates
news.text:
TORONTO (AP) — Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday, an official familiar with the plans told The Associated Press, escalating a trade fight that has sharply worsened since negotiations with the Trump administration collapsed.

The official spoke Monday on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the plans publicly.

Prime Minister Mark Carney had said Saturday that retaliation would target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, but he said Monday that Canada may instead use more targeted measures.

President Donald Trump escalated the dispute again Monday, telling Canadian leaders to “fall in line” or face consequences “far WORSE” than tariffs already imposed and threatening new 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel.

Earlier Monday, Carney accused Washington of trying to subordinate Canada and said U.S. trade demands had confirmed Canada’s fears that the United States was seeking to dismantle major Canadian industries.

“An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States” is “not something we’re going to accept,” Carney said.

He said Canada was willing to resume talks when Washington returned with “the right attitude.”

Carney was blunter in French.

“We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum,” Carney said. “That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal.”

The fiery words from both sides show how U.S.-Canada relations have deteriorated since Carney walked away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration late Friday, triggering the president’s threatened 50% tariffs the next day on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.

Carney cast doubt on the U.S.'s dependability, saying Canada was finding reliable partners “everywhere in the world, except in the United States. Except in the United States. And Russia.”

Trump unleashes personal attacks on Canadian leaders

On Monday, Trump came back with further tariffs, warning that he would impose them on Canada’s auto industry beginning next year.

“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote on social media, criticizing what he called the country’s “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers.

Carney said Washington’s auto-sector proposals would gradually have the effect of dismantling Canadian production.

“This is the most successful automotive partnership in history,” Carney said, referring to the deeply integrated Canada-U.S. industry.

Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unleashed his own tirade. In an interview with The Associated Press, he said Trump had underestimated Canadians’ willingness to endure economic pain rather than give in to U.S. pressure.

“We’re all in,” Ford said. “Up here, we’re at a fever pitch; everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice.”

Trump responded in a social media post by attacking Ford personally, calling him “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford,” and once again referring to Canada’s prime minister as “Governor Carney.”

Ford dismissed the insults: “If you think an insult from him hurts me? Well, bring it on, buddy, I’m ready.”

Ford is a Progressive Conservative whose party differs from that of Carney, a Liberal, but the two underscore broad political unity in Canada over the trade fight with Trump.

Ford threatens critical minerals and electricity

Ford said “everything is on the table” if the dispute worsens, including cutting off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario.

Critical minerals are increasingly important to U.S. national security and manufacturing. The Pentagon has sought more secure supplies of minerals used in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics as Washington tries to reduce reliance on China, which dominates the mining or processing of several strategically important minerals.

Ford said Canada should also consider increasingly severe retaliation if Trump continues targeting Canadian industries, including oil and potash, while Ontario could raise electricity prices or stop sending power south.

“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses,” Ford said. “Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes.”

Ford has used electricity as leverage before. During an earlier phase of the dispute, Ontario imposed a 25% surcharge on electricity exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York. Trump responded by threatening to double tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum before both sides backed away.

Auto industry becomes a central battleground

Ford accused Trump of not simply seeking a better trade deal but aiming to hollow out Canadian industries and move production south.

Ford said Trump wants to make Canada a vassal state.

“He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the U.S.,” Ford said.

The auto sector is especially important to Ontario, the center of Canada’s vehicle manufacturing industry. Plants and suppliers in Ontario are tightly integrated with factories in Michigan and other U.S. states, with parts routinely crossing the border multiple times during production.

Automakers including Ford, General Motors and Stellantis operate major assembly plants in Ontario, and the wider supply chain supports tens of thousands of jobs. Trump’s new threat of a 50% tariff on Canadian vehicles and parts puts that sector directly at the center of the escalating dispute.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Monday that “the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place” was because of the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada used access to its market to encourage vehicle production north of the border.

Ford says he opposed preliminary deal

Ford also disclosed that he had opposed the preliminary agreement Carney was considering before Canada walked away from negotiations, and that he was unwilling to restore American liquor to Ontario store shelves as part of an agreement.

“I wasn’t going to put the booze back on the shelves,” Ford said. “I was ready to go out there and call a press conference … and say I’m not buckling over.”

Ford said he understood Washington had sought language late in the negotiations that would have restricted Canada’s ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries without U.S. approval. Carney has called that demand unacceptable and a question of Canadian sovereignty.

Carney said the dispute also exposed a deeper divide over language and culture, saying protections for French and Canadian culture that Washington views as trade irritants are considered fundamental rights in Canada.

“Who does he think he is?” Ford said of Trump. “You gotta be kidding.”

Associated Press writer Seung Min Kim contributed from Washington.
news.author: Ebony Davis

news.title: Report Finds FEMA Deliberately Skipped Homes With Trump Signs
news.text:
FEMA relief workers who intentionally passed over homes displaying support for Donald Trump after Hurricane Milton violated both federal law and agency rules, according to a sharply critical government watchdog report obtained by Our News Outlet.

The findings, released Monday by the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, substantiate allegations that some disaster response workers made politically motivated decisions in the weeks before the 2024 presidential election. The report also shows that employees cited “Trump flag” in official records as the reason for skipping hurricane victims.

The extraordinary review, based on an internal audit of FEMA’s response to the October 2024 hurricane, confirms a key claim made by a whistleblower who brought the scandal to light shortly after Trump’s 2024 election victory. It also points to serious breakdowns within the federal agency tasked with delivering disaster aid to Americans in crisis.

The report’s headline was unequivocal: “FEMA Disaster Response Crew Violated Law and Policy by Skipping Homes with Political Signage.”

Using surveys filed by crew members at the time, investigators confirmed 11 cases in late October 2024 in which disaster workers bypassed properties for improper reasons. In one entry cited in the report, a worker wrote that the team “did not visit due to Trump flag.”

That figure may account for only a small share of the homes that were actually missed, an insider told Our News Outlet, noting that most of the related notes were left blank.

A source told Our News Outlet that the crew members’ conduct breached FEMA policy and the Hatch Act, the federal law restricting political activity by government employees. Violations can result in civil penalties, including termination, fines and forfeiture of pay.

“This is unacceptable for any public servant,” a DHS official said. “Federal disaster responses are supposed to serve every American equally, no matter who they voted for or what sign is in their yard.”

‘These actions crossed a line that should never be tolerated, especially during a disaster when people are at their most vulnerable and counting on their government to show up and help when they need it most.’

The scandal came to light days after the 2024 election, when the Daily Wire reported on internal messages in which a FEMA supervisor told workers to ‘avoid homes advertising Trump’ as they worked around Lake Placid, Florida. 

The crew bypassed at least 20 homes due to the guidance passed down by Washington, the publication reported.

FEMA Supervisor Marn’i Washington, who reportedly relayed the message in a group chat and verbally, was later fired along with three crew members.

Republicans in Congress and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis made sweeping claims accusing the Biden administration of deliberately denying disaster aid to Trump supporters. 

Upon taking office, Trump cited the case in signing an executive order creating a council to review ‘serious concerns of political bias in FEMA.’

FEMA’s Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR), releasing its own review in March 2025, ‘found no evidence that this was a systemic problem, nor that it was directed by agency or field leadership,’ according to a Politico report at the time.

However, the IG came down hard on officials for failing to properly train and supervise disaster responders, and fully document survivor interactions.

The watchdog, which recommends an overhaul of the system, said the problems continued under former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem’s leadership.

The Inspector General claimed DHS made their job more difficult by restricting investigators’ access to records and information.

It also faulted leadership for allowing a contract for FEMA’s Field Assessment and Collection Tools to lapse in September 2025, when then Secretary Kristi Noem did not act on FEMA’s request to fund it.

‘We requested access to the data in March 2025, but FEMA delays prevented us from obtaining the data prior to the contractor abruptly shutting down the system,’ the IG states.

The 10-page report found that most DHS crew leaders and members they interviewed ‘demonstrated no clear understanding of the Hatch Act,’ and that ‘FEMA DSA (Disaster Survivor Assistance) training did not cover ethics rules or Hatch Act provisions.’

‘FEMA DSA policies and procedure did not require crews to add details for why they skipped locations,’ the report adds.

The report found that FEMA crews canvassed 744,000 properties for Hurricane Milton and Hurricane Helene, which struck in late September. 

‘According to the FEMA Administrator at the time of the hurricanes and an internal FEMA investigation, after Hurricane Milton, a crew leader instructed their team to avoid homes advertising support for then-Presidential candidate Donald Trump. 

‘We conducted this audit to determine the extent to which FEMA followed its policies and procedures when canvassing communities impacted by Hurricanes Helene and Milton for the DSA program.’

It wasn’t until October 28 – nine days after the initial entry – that FEMA OPR became aware of the violations, when it received a whistleblower complaint. 

‘We reviewed the daily summary reports for the days the crew skipped 11 homes for unallowable reasons and confirmed they did not contain information on skipping homes due to political signage,’ the agency reports.

The workers were part of a DHS team that was supplemented by volunteers from other agencies.

According to The Daily Wire, one of the workers said: ‘I thought we could go help and make a difference. When we got there we were told to discriminate against people.

‘It’s almost unbelievable to think that somebody in the federal government would think that’s okay.’

A White House spokesperson said: ‘Under Biden, FEMA employees violated FEMA policy and the Hatch Act by refusing aid to disaster survivors who displayed political signs supporting President Trump. No Americans should ever be denied disaster aid because of their political beliefs.’

At the time, a FEMA spokesperson said: ‘While we believe this is an isolated incident, we have taken measures to remove the employee from their role and are investigating the matter to prevent this from happening ever again.

‘The employee who issued this guidance had no authority and was given no direction to tell teams to avoid these homes and we are reaching out to the people who may have not been reached as a result of this incident.’

The statement continued: ‘This is a matter that we take extremely seriously and we are doing everything we can to make sure all survivors receive support from FEMA.

‘We are horrified that this took place and therefore have taken extreme actions to correct this situation and have ensured that the matter was addressed at all levels.’

news.title: Canada could cut off electricity to the US, official says: 'Everything's on the table'
news.text: Canadians aren't playing around. Doug Ford, premier of Ontario, Canada's most populous province, says Canada is willing to go much further in the escalating trade war with the US than President Donald Trump realizes. "We can put massive pain on the US," Ford told reporters during a searing press conference on Monday. "President Trump underestimates us, and that's the biggest mistake: underestimating your opponent." If the trade war continues to ramp up, Ford said "everything's on the table," including electricity, critical minerals, and fuel. He added that Canadian premiers, who lead Canada's 10 provinces, needed to work together to put pressure on the US. "We need everyone to be on Team Canada and throw everything and the kitchen sink at them," he said. Trump's latest round of tariffs on Canada took effect on Saturday after talks between the North American allies fell through. The tariffs impact a range of Canadian goods, from alcohol and hockey equipment to paper and construction materials. Canada supplies electricity to the US via cross-border transmission lines. In 2025, Canada exported $3.3 billion worth of electricity to the US, according to Canadian government figures. Over 20 states import electricity from Canada, with New York, Michigan, Washington, Minnesota, and North Dakota among the largest importers, according to Canadian export data from June. New York and Michigan were the largest importers of electricity from Ontario. In an interview with The Associated Press on Monday, Ford said he could cut off electricity exports from Ontario to the US entirely. "Up here, we're at a fever pitch; everyone's in for an economic war," he told AP. "They know they're going to have to sacrifice." During the press conference, Ford pointed to several other Canadian products imported by the US that could be leveraged in the trade dispute, including oil, nickel, uranium, and potash. "He wants to put pain on Canadians? We'll leverage every bit of pain we possibly can on Americans," he said. Ford also doubled down on a comment he made earlier on Monday during a radio interview in which he said Trump can "kiss my ass." Trump has also ramped up his rhetoric and threats in the trade war. The president said Monday that starting January 1, 2027, tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts, and steel would be increased to 50%. Trump also called out Ford directly. "Lots of 'bluster' from Doug Ford, who is the Premier of the Canadian Province of Ontario, but who is better known as the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford," Trump said in a Truth Social post. The White House did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Tensions between the US and Canada have been strained since early 2025, when Trump levied broad tariffs on goods from Canada and Mexico. Canadians responded by boycotting some US goods and avoiding travel to the US. The latest tariffs have renewed calls for Canadians to boycott American goods. Canada is expected to announce its own retaliatory tariffs on the US. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the country will match US tariffs "dollar-for-dollar" starting September 8.
news.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford said "everything's on the table" in the US-Canada trade war, including electricity, critical minerals, and fuel.
news.author: Kelsey Vlamis

news.title: Trump’s nutrition advisor says kids should eat food fresh from the ground - like hot dogs
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s nutrition adviser has said kids should eat food fresh from the ground, and then suggested hot dogs as an option. 

During an event to promote nutritious school meals from local farmers on Monday, Dr. Ben Carson talked about teaching children where their food comes from and having them taste veggies straight from the soil. 

“I remember not too many months ago, [Agriculture] Secretary [Brooke] Rollins and I went to a school, and we were giving the children whole milk. They were just so amazed. They said, ‘I didn’t know milk could taste this good!’

“And what if we introduced them to food fresh from the ground? Teaching them — making these relationships with the farmers so they learn about the soil. They learn about irrigation. They learn about the effect that it has on their crop,” Carson said.

Carson then listed some examples of food children could eat on these farms, with one processed meat catching the audience’s attention.

“They get an opportunity to eat a tomato fresh off the vine. It’s a different food than you get in the store, quite frankly. Fresh sweet corn and hot dogs,” Carson said to laughter. “But what a difference it makes when they can taste these things. They won’t have a craving for the unhealthy foods that are so prevalent in our society.”

Carson, a former neurosurgeon and an opponent of Trump during the 2016 presidential election, was sworn in as the national advisor for nutrition, health and housing at the Department of Agriculture last September. He also served as Trump’s Department of Housing and Urban Development secretary during his first presidential term. 

His comment about feeding children hot dogs for a nutritious lunch is the latest flub from a Trump official attempting to carry out the goals of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, which scrutinizes ultra-processed foods. 

In late July, Kennedy grossly underestimated ingredient costs while presenting a recipe on his cooking show, The Real Food Show, which is focused on healthy, affordable meals. Instead of calculating how much it costs to buy the whole ingredient, just the price of each serving of the ingredient needed for the recipe was shown. 

As Washington Post columnist Monica Hesse noted in an article, “that kind of practical thinking is not helpful to a parent who has $20 in cash to get them to tomorrow’s paycheck.

“Safeway does not let you walk in, scoop some mayo out of a jar and pay one dollar at the cash register. You have to buy the whole thing.”

Rollins was also roasted earlier this year for suggesting Americans eat “a piece of chicken, a piece of broccoli, corn tortilla and one other thing” as a budget meal.

“‘You should eat prison meals’ prob not the best message,” Variety’s Chief Correspondent Marlow Stern wrote on X at the time.

Carson was at the Agriculture Department’s Washington, D.C. headquarters on Monday to support Rollins and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s new “Harvest to Hallways” initiative as part of the administration’s MAHA agenda.

The initiative will include a $50 million investment in school cafeterias, which, in part, will help pay for new equipment and up to $25 million in grants for schools to provide kids with locally grown foods. 

These investments in healthy school lunches come at a time when a packed lunch for children costs more than $6, and Americans struggle to pay for their grocery bills. 

While many school districts do offer some kind of cafeteria lunch for free, or at a reduced price, fewer children automatically qualify due to changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program made under the Trump administration.
news.summary: Dr. Ben Carson was promoting healthy school lunches that mean pupils ‘won’t have a craving for the unhealthy foods’
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Trump spoke with Pakistan Army Chief Munir last week ahead of Tehran visit: Report
news.text:
Washington DC [US], August 25 (ANI): US President Donald Trump spoke by phone with Pakistan Army Chief Asim Munir last week, before Munir's Tehran visit on Monday, according to CNN. A source familiar with the conversation confirmed to CNN that Trump spoke with Munir last week and discussed Iran with the Pakistani Army chief. Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported that Munir met with Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, who said the United States "must change its behaviour".According to IRIB, Rezaei emphasised Iran's security management of the Strait of Hormuz and said, "The United States must change its behaviour and take practical steps to implement the terms of the memorandum of understanding."According to IRIB, Rezaei referred to Pakistan's efforts to establish the14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). 

Earlier on Monday, Iran's Parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf met Pakistan Army Chief Asim Munir in Tehran during the latter's visit to the country and criticised the United States for its repeated breaches of its commitments under the 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed in June to end hostilities in West Asia and establish channels for technical talks, including on the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's nuclear programme.According to a statement shared by Ghalibaf on Telegram, the Iranian Parliamentary Speaker reviewed, along with Munir, the "numerous instances" of US breaches of commitments in implementing the MoU."The commitments of the parties in the Memorandum of Understanding are clear, and it was America that, by breaching its commitments, prevented the establishment of stability in the region and created another reason for distrust in this country," Ghalibaf said, as per the statement.The Iranian official also stressed that Tehran was continuing to pursue implementation of the MoU and said Iran was not being affected by external pressure."We are pursuing the implementation of the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding, and it is America that must adhere to its commitments based on the Memorandum of Understanding," the statement read.During the meeting, Munir also said that he would continue his efforts to restore stability in the region, according to the statement.Meanwhile, Munir arrived in Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian officials. His visit comes amid heightened regional tensions and continuing friction between Iran and the United States. (ANI)

news.title: Top court upholds Trump bid to curb mail-in ballots for now
news.text:
Donald Trump signed an executive order to restrict mail-in voting ahead of November’s midterm elections, drawing multiple legal challenges. (EPA Images pic)
WASHINGTON: The US Supreme Court gave president Donald Trump a temporary victory on Monday, lifting a lower court block on his executive order curbing the use of mail-in ballots.
The Republican president signed an order in March seeking to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the November midterm elections but it was immediately met with multiple legal challenges.
Democratic-led states sued the administration on grounds that under the US Constitution, states - and not the federal government - retain broad control over the administration of elections.
A district court in Massachusetts blocked implementation of the executive order but the Supreme Court on Monday lifted the judge's stay, allowing parts of Trump's directive to go ahead for now.
"The District Court lacked jurisdiction to bar the Government from trying to implement" the executive order, the Supreme Court majority said in an unsigned opinion.
But the justices withheld final judgment on the merits of the case pending further litigation.
"The Court's disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful," they said. "On that score, time will tell."
The three liberal justices on the nine-member Supreme Court dissented.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat, called the decision a "disgrace," adding that Trump "wants to make it harder for Americans to vote so they don't hold him accountable for the skyrocketing costs, illegal war, and rampant corruption that are a hallmark of his administration."
California governor Gavin Newsom, who is widely tipped to be a Democratic presidential candidate in the next election, said his state would file another lawsuit over the matter.
Trump's March executive order would require the compilation of lists of eligible voters and for the US Postal Service to deliver ballots only to voters who are on the lists.
Trump has been a longtime critic of mail-in ballots but has frequently used them himself, including this month when he voted by mail in Florida's Republican primary.
Trump has for years claimed without evidence that mail-in voting is highly vulnerable to fraud, repeatedly linking it to his false assertion that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him by Democrat Joe Biden.
"Mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt," he said during a July speech on election security.
Polls show that Trump's Republican Party faces a serious threat of losing its narrow control of Congress in the midterm elections in November, particularly in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber.
If Democrats win, they have signaled they will block Trump's agenda and could move to impeach him for the third time.
news.summary: The US president has long claimed without evidence that mail-in voting remains vulnerable to fraud, linking it to his 2020 election loss.
news.author: AFP
